title: Data Wrangling & EDA for Prediction
subtitle: Real data arrives in eight tables, three date formats, and a thousand blanks. pandas joins, groupbys, and datetime features on Olist e-commerce — and how to spot the leak that makes a model look brilliant and ship useless

objectives.title: Assemble a Modeling Table from Many
objectives.description: Olist ships as eight CSVs: orders, items, payments, reviews, customers, sellers, products, geolocation. One row per order with the right columns is the deliverable — and a join that silently triples your rows is the trap.

objectives.title: Ask Questions with groupby
objectives.description: Late-delivery rate by state, review score by delivery delay, subscription rate by past outcome. EDA is not making charts — it is interrogating the data before the model does.

objectives.title: Name the Missingness
objectives.description: Missing completely at random, missing at random, missing not at random — three patterns in plain English, and why the third one is a feature rather than a problem.

objectives.title: Spot Target Leakage Before It Ships
objectives.description: Call duration predicts a bank deposit with AUC 0.91 — and is useless, because you only know it after the call ends. Three real leaks, and the one question that catches all of them.

agenda.title: Homework #0 Debrief & The Data Problem
agenda.description: Your prediction problems from Canvas, read aloud. Then the uncomfortable truth: in Session 1 the data came as one clean table. It never does. Tonight is about the 80% of the job that happens before fit().
bulletPoints: Kaggle 2022 survey: data scientists still report spending most of their time cleaning and organizing data
The modeling table: one row per prediction unit, features known at prediction time, one target column

agenda.title: Meet Olist: Eight Tables, One Question
agenda.description: About 100,000 Brazilian e-commerce orders from 2016–2018 across orders, items, payments, reviews, customers, sellers, products and geolocation. Business question: which orders will arrive late — and will the customer leave a one-star review?
bulletPoints: Read the schema first: which column links which table, and what is the grain of each
Frame it: unit = one order · target = delivered after the estimated date · horizon = at purchase · decision = proactive apology or upgraded shipping

agenda.title: Joins That Lie: merge, validate, count
agenda.description: Orders join to items one-to-many: an order with three items becomes three rows, and your late-delivery rate is now weighted by basket size. The fix is a habit: print the row count before and after every merge, and use validate='one_to_one' to make pandas refuse a bad join.
bulletPoints: merge(how='left', validate='one_to_one') — the argument nobody uses and everyone should
Aggregate the many side first (items → total price, item count), then join at the order grain

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, compare row counts with a neighbor.

agenda.title: EDA That Asks Questions
agenda.description: groupby, agg, and pivot_table as interview tools. Late-delivery rate by customer state, review score by days late, and datetime features pulled from the purchase timestamp: weekday, hour, month, and days-to-estimate. Every chart ends with a sentence a manager could act on.
bulletPoints: pd.to_datetime, then .dt.dayofweek, .dt.hour, and date arithmetic — three lines that create ten features
Missing values: TotalCharges is blank for exactly the 11 Telco customers with tenure 0 — that is a pattern, not noise

agenda.title: The Anatomy of a Leak
agenda.description: Bank Marketing: predicting whether a customer subscribes to a term deposit. Add call duration and AUC jumps from 0.76 to 0.91 — and the model is worthless, because duration is only known after the call in which the customer said yes. Three real leaks, one test: would you know this value at the moment you have to predict?
bulletPoints: Leak types: features recorded after the outcome, target proxies (refund amount for 'was refunded'), and test data bleeding into preprocessing
The prediction-time test: freeze the clock at the moment of decision and delete every column the clock hasn't reached

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Homework #1
agenda.description: The wrangling checklist: grain, join, validate, aggregate, datetime, missingness, leakage. Homework #1 applies it end to end on Telco with a baseline model.
bulletPoints: Next week: turning the modeling table into a leak-proof scikit-learn Pipeline
Homework #1 due Mon Sep 28 on Canvas

activities.title: From Eight Tables to One Modeling Table
activities.description: Build the Olist modeling table at the order grain: one row per order, total basket value, item count, customer state, purchase weekday and hour, and the target — delivered after the estimated date. Every merge is validated and counted.

steps.title: Know the grain
steps.description: orders is one row per order; order_items is one row per item. Print both shapes and the number of unique order_id in each. That difference is the trap.

steps.title: Aggregate the many side first
steps.description: groupby('order_id') on items to get item_count and basket_value. Now items is one row per order and the join is safe.

steps.title: Merge with validate
steps.description: orders.merge(items_agg, on='order_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one'). Print the row count before and after. They must match.

steps.title: Build the target and the time features
steps.description: late = delivered_date > estimated_date. Then weekday, hour, and month from the purchase timestamp. Check the late rate overall and by customer state.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd, kagglehub, os

path = kagglehub.dataset_download('olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce')
orders = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(path, 'olist_orders_dataset.csv'), parse_dates=[
    'order_purchase_timestamp', 'order_delivered_customer_date', 'order_estimated_delivery_date'])
items = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(path, 'olist_order_items_dataset.csv'))

print(len(orders), orders.order_id.nunique())   # one row per order
print(len(items),  items.order_id.nunique())    # many rows per order!

items_agg = (items.groupby('order_id')
                  .agg(item_count=('order_item_id', 'size'), basket_value=('price', 'sum'))
                  .reset_index())

df = orders.merge(items_agg, on='order_id', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
assert len(df) == len(orders)

df['late'] = (df.order_delivered_customer_date > df.order_estimated_delivery_date).astype(int)
df['weekday'] = df.order_purchase_timestamp.dt.dayofweek
df['hour'] = df.order_purchase_timestamp.dt.hour
print(df['late'].mean())

activities.discussionNote: Notice which columns you are not allowed to use: the actual delivery date builds the target, so anything derived from it — days late, carrier hand-off date — is a leak. The clock stops at order_purchase_timestamp. Everything the model sees must exist at that moment.

activities.title: Reproduce the Leak: Bank Marketing and Call Duration
activities.description: 45,211 phone calls from a Portuguese bank's deposit campaign; 11.7% said yes. Fit the same logistic regression twice — once with call duration, once without — and watch a worthless feature produce a spectacular score.

steps.title: Fit without duration
steps.description: Age, balance, job, prior-campaign outcome and the rest. Cross-validated AUC lands around 0.76.

steps.title: Fit with duration
steps.description: Add the length of the call. AUC jumps to about 0.91. A manager would be thrilled.

steps.title: Apply the prediction-time test
steps.description: When do we need the prediction? Before dialing, to choose whom to call. Is call duration known then? No. Delete it, and explain why the 0.91 was a lie.

activities.discussionNote: The UCI documentation for this dataset says it outright: duration 'highly affects the output target' and 'should be discarded if the intention is to have a realistic predictive model.' Most datasets don't come with that warning. Your job is to write it yourself.

takeaways.text: The deliverable of wrangling is a modeling table: one row per prediction unit, features known at prediction time, one target column. Get the grain right and everything downstream gets easier.
Joins lie silently. Aggregate the many side first, merge with validate=, and print the row count before and after. A model trained on tripled rows is a model trained on a different population.
Leakage is the #1 way smart people build useless models. Freeze the clock at the moment of decision and delete every column the clock hasn't reached — call duration, refund amount, days late.

homework.label: Homework #1
homework.text: Due Mon Sep 28, before class, on Canvas. Using the Telco churn data from the Session 1 notebook: (1) fix the TotalCharges column (it is stored as text and is blank for the 11 customers with tenure 0 — decide what to do and justify it in one sentence); (2) produce three groupby tables that each answer a business question about who churns (contract, internet service, payment method are good starts), with one sentence of interpretation each; (3) engineer at least two new features (for example number of add-on services, or average monthly charge over tenure) and explain why they might carry signal; (4) list every column you would have to drop if the prediction were made at sign-up rather than today, and why; (5) refit the Session 1 logistic regression with your new features and report accuracy, the confusion matrix, and the baseline. Submit the notebook with outputs visible.
